newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: One AIRC judge dissents in Australia wage decision.
newsitem.headline: One AIRC judge dissents in Australia wage decision.

text.p: The seven-person Australian Industrial Relations Commission's (AIRC) decision to increase wages for the lowest paid workers by A$10 a week was not unanimous, with Vice President Iain Ross registering a dissenting decision.
Ross said he would have awarded those currently paid below A$503.80 a week a A$15 a week increase and set a 2.5 percent across-the-board increase for those paid more than A$503.80 a week.

Ross said the government's submissions had overstated the affect of a A$15 a week pay rise for the lower paid on Average Weekly Ordinary Time Earnings (AWOTE). The government said a A$15 a week pay rise would raise AWOTE by 0.60 percent, while a A$10 a week rise would raise AWOTE by 0.34 percent.
Ross said the inflation environment was relatively positive and could have coped with the wage increases he recommended.

"The improved outlook for business investment and the lower than originally forecast level of inflation and wages growth are particularly significant," Ross said in his 110 page section of the 273 page report.
"The major economic indicators considered are reasonably positive, or, at least, do not suggest any basis for undue caution in addressing the claims before the commission," he said.
Ross also said the decreasing importance of administered or award wages in the economy meant his A$15/2.5 percent increase would not have an undue effect on the economy.
"Commission decisions to adjust the award safety net no have impact on aggregate wagers which is much less than that from others sources such as enterprise bargaining," he said.
Earlier the majority of the commission said about a third of employees were award wage-earners, down from about a half in 1994 and two thirds in 1993.
